Under FCC review now
Two filings are driving the decision
SpaceX · Orbital Data Center System
1,000,000
satellites, filed 30 January 2026
  • 500–2,000 km, kept sunlit for power
  • Seeks milestone and bond waivers
  • Pitched as relief for AI compute
Reflect Orbital · “Sunlight on demand”
50,000
mirror satellites planned by 2035
  • FCC application: demo satellite Eärendil-1
  • Mirrors ~18–55 m, ground spots ≥5 km
  • Tests at 0.1–2.3 lux: moonlight or brighter
  • 1,800+ comments by March 2026
Sources: FCC DA 26-113; SAT-LOA-20250701-00129; AAS/AIBS docket summaries
03
SpaceX’s response to the record
Promised mitigations, and what’s missing
What SpaceX says it will do
  • Aim to stay fainter than magnitude 7
  • Shade and off-point arrays and radiators
  • Develop infrared guidelines with NSF
  • Share ephemerides roughly hourly
  • Phase deployment, starting smaller
  • Time re-entries around science campaigns
Builds on Starlink: dark paint, mirror film, attitude biasing
What’s still missing
  • Most Starlinks still miss magnitude 7
  • No plan for aggregate sky brightness
  • No brightness-model results published
  • Infrared commitment left vague
  • No deorbit timeline in the filing
  • Argues NEPA review does not apply
Voluntary and unquantified: exactly what Option C would turn into binding licence conditions.
Sources: SpaceX Consolidated Opposition, 16 Mar 2026; AAS Reply, Mar 2026; SpaceX Starlink brightness briefing, 2023
04
The physics
Two ways satellites degrade the sky
Trails
A sunlit satellite streaks across an exposure. Scheduling can dodge some: Rubin modelling halves streaked visits, at the cost of ~10% of observing time.
Diffuse brightening
Faint satellites and scattered light lift the whole sky background. No schedule avoids it: it belongs to the constellation, not to any one track.
Licensing that accepts scheduling as mitigation leaves the second harm untouched.
Sources: Hainaut 2026; Hu et al., ApJL 2022
05
The evidence base
Independent studies point the same way
Ground
28%
of VLT field of view lost, at worst, under SpaceX’s filing; mirrors lift the sky 3–4×
Hainaut, A&A 2026
Space
~40%
of Hubble images trailed at ~56,000 satellites; up to 96% for newer telescopes
Borla et al., Nature 2025
Archives
2×
rise in trailed images at China’s Xinglong 80-cm telescope, 2019–2023
Ren et al. 2026; Kruk et al. 2023
Atmosphere
5 yrs
deorbited after ~5 years, not 25, so re-entries and ozone impact are rising
Ferreira 2024; Barker 2026
Different instruments, methods and research groups. The question is no longer is there harm? but how much harm is tolerable, and how is it priced?

07
The one number regulators can use
~100,000
satellites in total — and only if every one stays fainter than magnitude 7.
Brightness and population trade off against each other. A numeric cap alone, or a brightness rule alone, is not enough: they have to be licensed together, across operators.
Hainaut, ESO / Astronomy & Astrophysics, July 2026 · magnitude 7 ≈ the naked-eye limit at a dark site

10
The governance gap
Nobody is pricing the externality
In the United States
  • Constellations treated as NEPA-exempt
  • GAO 2022: basis never documented
  • Critics: FCC 25-47 would narrow it further
Internationally
  • Outer Space Treaty: silent on brightness
  • COPUOS: consensus, non-binding
  • ITU: radio spectrum, not light
  • IAU CPS: coordinates, cannot enforce
No body has binding authority over optical brightness or cumulative debris. A US decision alone cannot bind systems licensed elsewhere.
Sources: GAO-23-105005; FCC 25-47; UNOOSA; IAU CPS
11
Why act before deployment
Some of these harms cannot be undone
A licensing decision
Reversible. It can be conditioned, staged, revisited or revoked as evidence comes in.
A debris cascade or ozone step-change
One-way. Once a Kessler cascade or mass re-entry chemistry is triggered, no regulator can reverse it.
So thresholds belong before deployment, not after harm is observed.
Sources: Kessler & Cour-Palais 1978; Boley & Byers 2021; Barker et al. 2026

13
For this room
Three things Europe can lead on
01
Carry the global standard
Back a COPUOS brightness-and-debris guideline, with IAU CPS as technical coordinator, so no single licence is undone elsewhere.
02
Bring evidence from 50°N
Feed European impact data into licensing processes, rather than relying on figures modelled for Chile.
03
Price the night sky
Value dark-sky access and nocturnal ecosystems, and cost re-entry ozone loss like carbon, so both sides of the ledger count.
